title: Bacteria, Not Fertilizer, Use the Oxygen

scenes.tts: Each summer, the Chesapeake Bay's deep channel typically has too little oxygen near the bottom. Crabs and fish cannot stay. People call it a dead zone. No one pours in a chemical that soaks up oxygen. So how can fertilizer on fields far up rivers such as the Susquehanna, Potomac, and James take oxygen from the Bay's floor? Can people fix it?
scenes.visual: Cross-section of the Bay: bottom water turns red as crab and fish leave; a crossed-out oxygen-soaking chemical; fertilizer on land, a question mark, and the bottom water.
scenes.narration: Each summer, the Chesapeake Bay's deep channel typically has too little oxygen near the bottom. Crabs and fish cannot stay. People call it a dead zone. No one pours in a chemical that soaks up oxygen. So how can fertilizer on fields far up rivers such as the Susquehanna, Potomac, and James take oxygen from the Bay's floor? Can people fix it?

scenes.tts: A watershed is all the land that drains into one river, lake or bay. Runoff is rainwater that flows over the ground and carries what it picks up. Part of what feeds the dead zone washes in from farms, lawns, wastewater plants and even the air. A nutrient is a substance living things need to grow. Here, that means nitrogen and phosphorus.
scenes.visual: Land and Bay: watershed outlined, rain and runoff arrow, farms, lawns, wastewater plant and air each send orange nutrient dots into the surface water.

Part of what feeds the dead zone washes in from farms, lawns, wastewater plants and even the air. A nutrient is a substance living things need to grow. Here, that means nitrogen and phosphorus.

scenes.tts: Extra nutrients make algae grow fast. A sudden, thick growth of algae is an algal bloom. The green water blocks sunlight from underwater grasses, and algae growing on the grass blades shade them too. Then the algae die and sink to the bottom. A decomposer is a living thing that breaks down dead matter.
scenes.visual: Green dots multiply in the surface water; sunlight rays stop at the green band and the grass dims; the dots turn grey and sink.
scenes.narration: Extra nutrients make algae grow fast. A sudden, thick growth of algae is an algal bloom. The green water blocks sunlight from underwater grasses, and algae growing on the grass blades shade them too. Then the algae die and sink to the bottom. A decomposer is a living thing that breaks down dead matter.

scenes.tts: Bacteria decompose the dead algae, and they use oxygen as they do. Dissolved oxygen is oxygen gas mixed into water. Fish and crabs take it in through their gills. Low oxygen in bottom water is called hypoxia. Animals that can swim away leave. Others may sicken or die. The fertilizer never takes oxygen itself. Living things use it.
scenes.visual: Bacteria among the dead algae pull blue oxygen dots out of the bottom water; fish and crab; hypoxia tint; fish leave, crab dims; crossed arrow from fertilizer, bacteria glow.

scenes.tts: Why the deep channel, and why summer? In summer, fresh river water floats on saltier, heavier seawater. The layers mix poorly, so little new oxygen reaches the bottom. Warm water also holds less dissolved oxygen, and bacteria decompose faster when it is warm, so they use oxygen faster. Eutrophication is the enrichment of water with nutrients. It feeds too much algae growth and can lead to oxygen loss.
scenes.visual: Two layers labelled; an oxygen arrow from the air stops at the layer boundary; two bars compare cooler and warm water; then a three-chip chain: nutrients, too much algae, oxygen loss.

scenes.tts: So how do human actions change the Bay, and what can we do? People add many of those nutrients, so people can cut them. A riparian forest buffer is a strip of trees and shrubs along a stream. It slows runoff and traps soil, and its roots hold the bank in place. Plants and soil microbes also remove nitrate from water seeping through the ground beneath it. Cover crops and wastewater upgrades also cut nutrients. Oyster reefs shelter other animals, but they do not replace cutting nutrients. Underwater grass has partly returned. Recovery is real, but slow and usually partial, and results often lag by years.
scenes.visual: Land with a lime buffer strip stopping orange dots; cover crop and wastewater chips; an oyster reef; grass partly regrowing; a timeline arrow labelled years.
